cards.front: What may a driver facing a circular green do, and who yields on a left turn?
cards.back: A driver facing a circular green signal may enter the intersection and go straight, turn right or turn left unless signs or pavement markings prohibit a movement, every turn follows the right-of-way rules, and a left turn on circular green must yield to oncoming vehicles.

cards.front: What does a green arrow allow, and what does a left-turn green arrow usually mean?
cards.back: A green arrow, shown alone or with other indications, lets drivers enter the intersection to make the movement the arrow shows, and a green arrow in a left-turn signal usually means that opposing traffic is stopped.

cards.front: What does a steady circular yellow or yellow arrow mean, and when may you drive through?
cards.back: A steady circular yellow means the green is ending and will change to red, you should drive through a yellow only if your vehicle is already within the intersection clearance, and a yellow arrow means the green arrow is ending and will change to red.

cards.front: What must traffic facing a steady circular red do, and what is the only exception?
cards.back: Traffic facing a steady circular red must stop unless making a movement permitted by a green arrow, and must remain stopped until another indication allows it to proceed, the only exception being a permitted turn on red.

cards.front: When may a driver turn right or left on red?
cards.back: A driver may turn right on red at the intersection of two-way streets, or turn left on red from a one-way street onto another one-way street, but only after yielding to all other traffic and pedestrians and only where no sign prohibits the turn.

cards.front: What does a steady red arrow require?
cards.back: A steady red arrow requires a complete stop before the intersection, stop line or crosswalk for the direction the arrow shows, and the driver must remain stopped as long as the arrow is red.

cards.front: How does a steady circular red differ from a steady red arrow?
cards.back: A steady circular red still allows a permitted turn on red after yielding, whereas a steady red arrow means remaining stopped for that direction as long as the arrow stays red.

cards.front: How does a left turn on circular green differ from one on a green arrow?
cards.back: A left turn on a circular green must yield to oncoming vehicles, while a left-turn green arrow usually means the opposing traffic is stopped.

cards.front: When is turning right on red allowed, and when turning left on red?
cards.back: Turning right on red is allowed at an intersection of two-way streets, but turning left on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, both after yielding and absent a prohibiting sign.

cards.front: What do pavement markings do, and what do white and yellow lines separate?
cards.back: Pavement markings warn, regulate and inform traffic like highway signs, white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction, and yellow lines separate lanes moving in opposite directions.

cards.front: What do broken yellow lines mean, and when may you pass?
cards.back: Broken yellow lines separate traffic moving in opposite directions, and when the broken yellow line is on your side of the road you may pass when it is safe.

cards.front: What does a solid yellow line on your side mean, and where does it mark the left edge?
cards.back: Solid yellow lines also separate opposing traffic, a solid yellow line on your side of the road means you must not pass, and on interstates, one-way streets and divided four-lane roads a solid yellow line marks the left edge of the pavement.

cards.front: How are same-direction lanes separated, and how do you drive within them?
cards.back: On roadways with more than one lane moving in the same direction the lanes are separated by broken white lines, sometimes with broken black lines added for visibility, and you drive within the lines and never straddle them except when changing lanes.

cards.front: What do solid white lines mark, and what do they forbid between lanes?
cards.back: Solid white lines mark the edge of the pavement and help you stay on the road at night or in bad weather, and where solid white lines separate lanes moving in the same direction you do not change lanes.

cards.front: What are center left-turn lanes for, and how do you recognize them?
cards.back: Center left-turn lanes are reserved for left turns from either direction and are never through or passing lanes, and you recognize them by the solid yellow lines nearest the through lanes with broken yellow lines to the left of them.

cards.front: How are reversible lanes marked, and what makes them unique?
cards.back: Reversible lanes, used where traffic is heavy at certain times of day, are marked on both sides by a double broken yellow line, and this is the only case in which a driver may drive for any distance to the left of a yellow line.

cards.front: How do broken and solid yellow lines on your side differ for passing?
cards.back: A broken yellow line on your side permits passing when safe, but a solid yellow line on your side forbids passing entirely.

cards.front: How do broken and solid white lines between lanes differ?
cards.back: A broken white line between same-direction lanes allows a lane change without straddling, whereas a solid white line between same-direction lanes means do not change lanes.

cards.front: How does a reversible lane differ from a center left-turn lane?
cards.back: A reversible lane bordered on both sides by double broken yellow lines is the only place a driver may travel left of a yellow line, while a center left-turn lane with solid yellow outside and broken yellow inside is for left turns only.

cards.front: What do intersection flashers show for each direction?
cards.back: At certain intersections flashers supplement or replace stop signs, showing circular flashing red in all directions or circular flashing yellow for the through traffic.

cards.front: What do a circular flashing yellow and a circular flashing red each require?
cards.back: A driver facing a circular flashing yellow may proceed through the intersection with caution, while a circular flashing red is the same as a stop sign and requires a complete stop and yielding to all other traffic and pedestrians.

cards.front: When are signals placed in flashing operation, and how do they then work?
cards.back: When traffic control signals are not needed or are out of order they may be placed in flashing operation, and they then work the same as intersection flashers.

cards.front: What do a green arrow, yellow X and red X over a lane each mean?
cards.back: Lane use control signals show a green downward arrow when traffic may use the lane under it, a yellow X when the lane is about to close or reverse direction and you should move out as soon as you can, and a red X when the lane is closed or carrying opposing traffic and must not be used.

cards.front: Where are special lane signals used, and what do they indicate?
cards.back: Special lane signals are used where the direction of a street or of certain lanes changes during the day, and they indicate how each lane may be used.

cards.front: How do circular flashing yellow and flashing red differ?
cards.back: A circular flashing yellow means proceed with caution, but a circular flashing red is treated exactly like a stop sign with a complete stop and yielding.

cards.front: How does a yellow X over a lane differ from a red X?
cards.back: A yellow X over a lane warns that the lane is about to close or reverse so you should leave it soon, while a red X means the lane is already closed or carrying opposing traffic and must not be used.

cards.front: What do railroad crossing signs look like, and what does the sign below a crossbuck show?
cards.back: Railroad crossing signs may be round or diamond-shaped and yellow with black symbols, or black letters on white bars in the shape of an X called a crossbuck, and a sign below the crossbuck gives the number of tracks when there are two or more.

cards.front: What do crossing devices signal, and what happens if you fail to stop when they activate?
cards.back: Some railroad crossings have electrical devices such as bells, flashers and automatic gates to signal an approaching train, you must yield to all trains, and failing to stop when the lights are flashing or a barrier is down results in a citation.

cards.front: What should you do at multiple tracks, and when may you enter a crossing?
cards.back: Where there are two or more tracks you must be alert for a second train on the other set of tracks, and you should not enter a crossing until the vehicle ahead has moved far enough that you can clear the tracks, or you may be trapped and hit by another vehicle or a train.

cards.front: How does the yellow railroad warning differ from the crossbuck?
cards.back: The round or diamond yellow sign is the advance warning of a railroad crossing, while the white X crossbuck marks the crossing itself and a sign beneath it counts the tracks when there are two or more.

cards.front: What do the hand and walking figure crosswalk signals mean for pedestrians?
cards.back: Crosswalk signals are traffic signals for pedestrians who must obey them, a hand symbol or the words don't walk means pedestrians are not to cross, and a walking figure or the word walk means they may cross inside the crosswalk lines.

cards.front: What do crosswalks at intersections and school zones signal, and why be alert there?
cards.back: Crosswalks at intersections and in school zones signal a high pedestrian traffic zone, and being especially alert for pedestrians there reduces the risk of crashes.

cards.front: Who has the right-of-way on any road whether or not in a crosswalk?
cards.back: A blind person on foot who uses a guide dog or other service animal or carries a white cane or walking stick has the right-of-way on any highway, street or road whether or not in a crosswalk.

cards.front: What do white diamond shapes painted in a lane tell drivers?
cards.back: White diamond shapes painted in a lane tell drivers the lane is designated for car pools, bicycles or buses.

cards.front: How are crosswalks marked, where are they unmarked, and what must you not do?
cards.back: Many crosswalks are marked by solid white lines running all the way across the pavement at intersections and sometimes between them, some crosswalks especially in residential areas are unmarked, and you must not block a crosswalk with your car.

cards.front: What are stop lines, and where do you stop when there is none?
cards.back: Stop lines are wide white lines painted across the traffic lanes to mark where you must stop at an intersection, keeping you clear of pedestrians and cross traffic, and where there is no stop line or crosswalk you stop before entering the intersection where you can see traffic from all directions.

cards.front: How do walk signals work, and who has right-of-way regardless of crosswalk?
cards.back: The hand symbol or don't walk indication forbids pedestrians to cross while the walking figure or walk indication permits it, yet a blind pedestrian with a guide dog or white cane has the right-of-way everywhere regardless of a crosswalk.

cards.front: How do stop lines differ from crosswalk lines?
cards.back: Wide white stop lines mark exactly where to stop at an intersection, whereas solid white crosswalk lines run fully across the pavement and mark a space a car must never block.

recap_hooks.text: Remember circular green rules, green arrow meaning and steady yellow means ending
Remember white versus yellow lines, broken yellow allows passing and solid yellow forbids passing
Remember intersection flashers, flashing yellow versus red and signals in flashing operation
Remember railroad signs and crossbuck, yield to all trains and watch for a second train
Remember crosswalk signals, crosswalk high-pedestrian zones and blind pedestrian right-of-way
